the elastic and viscose modulus, as well as the damping coefficient and the dynamic stiffness of the degenerated disc are lower than the normal disc, and the degenerated disc shows higher stress concentration in the annulus and nucleus, especially in the posterior part of the disc, which is the main reason for disc herniation.

1) the disc degenerates with age, and the degeneration is characterized by a reduction in the elastic and viscose moduli, and a reduction in the dynamic parameters, 2) the disc degeneration can be classified as mild and severe, and 3) the disc degenerate in a nonlinear way, with the degeneration in the nucleus pulposus and the anulus fibrosus occurring at different rates.

the elastic and viscose moduli of the intervertebral discs in compression are age dependent and that the distribution of stresses in the discs is different in the degenerated and non-degenerated discs.

the study of the biomechanics of the human intervertebral discs, and in particular, the effect of loading history and age on the mechanical behaviour of the disc.
the biomechanics of the human intervertebral disc.

the development of a methodology that allows to investigate the biomechanics of a degenerated intervertebral disc in compression, with the aim to understand the role of loading history and age on the disc biomechanics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the disc with degeneration has less elastic modulus and more viscous modulus.
the degeneration of the disc is a complex process that depends on the loading history and age.
degeneration affects the biomechanical properties of the intervertebral disc, and that the disc is more sensitive to compression in the early stage of disc degeneration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

disc degeneration is associated with the decrease in disc height and the increase in disc area, and the disc degeneration can be evaluated with the disc height, the area of the nucleus pulposus and the disc height to disc area ratio.
disc degeneration can be evaluated by the biomechanical behavior of the disc, and the disc degeneration can also be predicted by the numerical model.
we can distinguish the disc biomechanics of degenerative discs from healthy discs by using a combination of experimental, anatomical, and numerical methods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the degenerated discs are stiffer and have a higher damping coefficient.
the degenerative disc is stiffer than a healthy disc, and that the disc is more susceptible to failure under cyclic loading than to static loading.
the biomechanics of degenerated intervertebral discs is not uniform throughout the disc.
